claim: GSAM publicly uses both 'OCIO' and 'fiduciary management' for this business in the UK, and says the terms are used interchangeably and mean different things in different geographies.
passage: Ed Francis, 'Head of International OCIO and UK Fiduciary Management Team' (2023, 2024); terms 'can mean different things in different geographies' (2024).
notes: GSAM's own distinction: OCIO = partial delegation with trustees keeping strategic asset allocation; fiduciary management = fuller delegation. Other firms and surveys (e.g. Isio) draw the line differently.

claim: Goldman Sachs reported $480bn of OCIO assets under supervision globally as of 31 March 2026.
passage: '$480 billion in OCIO assets under supervision (AUS) globally as of 3/31/2026'
notes: Global figure. No UK-only or EMEA-only OCIO figure is published. AUS is not the same as fee-earning discretionary AUM; the same release distinguishes OCIO AUM from assets under advisement.

claim: Earlier public OCIO scale markers: 'more than £200 billion' (Sept 2023), 'nearly $450bn' after Shell (Sept 2025), 'more than £300bn' (Nov 2025).
passage: 'Global OCIO assets under supervision ... more than £200 billion' (2023); 'nearly $450bn (£332bn)' (2025); 'oversees more than £300bn globally' (2025).
notes: Each figure comes from GS or a GS spokesperson via trade press; they are not independently audited OCIO league-table figures.

claim: The former intern's belief that OCIO exists only in the UK is not supported as a statement about Goldman Sachs: the OCIO business is global, with large US mandates and stated growth in the Netherlands, Germany and Switzerland.
passage: US: Verizon and Lockheed Martin OCIO mandates (July 2026); Europe: growth 'specifically in the UK, the Netherlands, Germany, and Switzerland'; title 'Head of EMEA OCIO Institutional Business'.
notes: What remains possible but unestablished: that within the London client-coverage organisation, the dedicated OCIO client team the intern saw sat inside or alongside the UK team. The EMEA-wide title on the Nov 2026 awards page points to an EMEA remit rather than a UK-only one.

claim: GS described itself in September 2023 as 'the second largest OCIO manager globally' and 'one of the largest in the UK'.
passage: 'the second largest OCIO manager globally' and 'one of the largest in the UK'
notes: Self-description in a press release with no ranking source cited. Verified only as a statement GS made; the ranking itself was not checked against an independent league table and may have changed since 2023.

passage: 'the team is still growing' (Kipling, Nov 2025)

claim: GSAM's UK fiduciary management push dates from late 2021, when it hired Ed Francis from Willis Towers Watson to lead the business; an early win was the £1.6bn Short Brothers Common Investment Fund (May 2022).

passage: 'There is also a fiduciary fee based on the asset value of the return seeking and CDI portfolios. The LDI manager charges the Scheme directly'

passage: 'BAE Systems' in-house investment management team will join Goldman Sachs Asset Management.'

A later change (2025/26) is possible but no announcement was found. Keep this company's name out of interview material and shareable outputs in connection with GS.

period: Transitions expected to complete later in 2025

claim: UK trust-based schemes must run a competitive tender, inviting bids from at least three unconnected providers, before fiduciary managers manage 20% or more of scheme assets; the duty has sat in pensions regulations overseen by TPR since 1 October 2022, replacing the CMA's 2019 Order.

notes: Explains why every UK OCIO appointment in the evidence mentions a tender and a third-party adviser (PwC, Isio, Barnett Waddingham, Redington). Public-sector contracting authorities follow procurement law instead.

passage: 'About 18% of UK schemes use some form of fiduciary management' (Isio 2023, data at 30 June 2023).

claim: GSAM's stated view (Nov 2025) is that OCIO has moved from small schemes to large ones with in-house teams, driven by sponsors questioning whether running pensions is core business, maturing schemes shifting to cashflow-driven and hedging strategies, and CIO succession gaps.

notes: s179 measures the cost of PPF-level compensation, lower than full buyout cost, so it overstates how many schemes could afford buyout.
